nyciml-2009-10-fall-junior-01.title: Check the pairings
nyciml-2009-10-fall-junior-01.body:
There are $6$ ways to pair the widths with the lengths. The best pairs largest with largest: $15\cdot9+12\cdot8+10\cdot7=135+96+70=301$. This is the Rearrangement Inequality: a sum of products is largest when both lists are sorted the same way.

**Answer: 301**

nyciml-2009-10-fall-junior-01.title: Swapping argument
nyciml-2009-10-fall-junior-01.body:
If a longer length is paired with a narrower width than a shorter length, swapping the two widths changes the area by $(L_1-L_2)(W_1-W_2)>0$ for $L_1>L_2$, $W_1>W_2$. So the sorted pairing is optimal, giving $301$.

**Answer: 301**

nyciml-2009-10-fall-junior-02.title: Choose teams in turn
nyciml-2009-10-fall-junior-02.body:
Choose the 3-person team in $\binom{12}{3}=220$ ways, then the 4-person team from the remaining $9$ in $\binom94=126$ ways; the rest form the 5-person team. Total $220\cdot126=27720$.

**Answer: 27720**

nyciml-2009-10-fall-junior-04.title: Self-similarity
nyciml-2009-10-fall-junior-04.body:
Let $x$ be the value. Then $x=\sqrt{20+x}$, so $x^2-x-20=0$, $(x-5)(x+4)=0$. Since $x>0$, $x=5$.

**Answer: 5**

nyciml-2009-10-fall-junior-04.title: Iterate
nyciml-2009-10-fall-junior-04.body:
The terms $\sqrt{20}\approx4.47$, $\sqrt{24.47}\approx4.95$, $\sqrt{24.95}\approx4.995,\dots$ increase toward the fixed point $5$ of $t\mapsto\sqrt{20+t}$.

**Answer: 5**

nyciml-2009-10-fall-junior-05.title: Middle term
nyciml-2009-10-fall-junior-05.body:
Write the numbers as $a-2,\dots,a+2$; the sum is $5a$, which is divisible by $15$ exactly when $3\mid a$. We need $a-2>1000$, so $a\ge1003$; the smallest multiple of $3$ is $1005$, giving sum $5025$.

**Answer: 5025**

nyciml-2009-10-fall-junior-05.title: Check multiples of 15
nyciml-2009-10-fall-junior-05.body:
The smallest possible sum is $1001+\dots+1005=5015$. Sums of five consecutive integers are multiples of $5$; the first multiple of $15$ at least $5015$ is $5025=1003+1004+1005+1006+1007$.

**Answer: 5025**

nyciml-2009-10-fall-junior-06.title: Similar triangles
nyciml-2009-10-fall-junior-06.body:
Extend $DA$ and $CB$ to meet at $P$. Let $J=[PAB]$ and $K=[ABFE]=[EFCD]$, and let $EF=x$. Triangles $PAB$, $PEF$, $PDC$ are similar, so
$$\frac{x^2}{6^2}=\frac{J+K}{J}=1+\frac KJ,\qquad \frac{10^2}{6^2}=\frac{J+2K}{J}=1+\frac{2K}{J}.$$
Hence $\frac{x^2}{36}-1=\frac12\left(\frac{100}{36}-1\right)$, so $x^2=\frac{36+100}{2}=68$ and $x=2\sqrt{17}$. (Only the bases matter.)

**Answer: $2\sqrt{17}$**

nyciml-2009-10-fall-junior-06.title: Quadratic mean
nyciml-2009-10-fall-junior-06.body:
In general the areas of the triangles at $P$ are proportional to the squares of the parallel sides, so $[PEF]$ is the average of $[PAB]$ and $[PDC]$: $x^2=\frac{a^2+b^2}{2}$. With $a=6$, $b=10$: $x=\sqrt{68}=2\sqrt{17}$.

**Answer: $2\sqrt{17}$**

nyciml-2009-10-fall-junior-07.title: Power of a Point
nyciml-2009-10-fall-junior-07.body:
Let $CE=x$. Then $AE=x-1$, $DE=x+1$, $BE=2x$, and $AE\cdot EB=CE\cdot ED$ gives $2x(x-1)=x(x+1)$. Since $x>0$, $2x-2=x+1$, so $x=3$. Then $AB=AE+EB=2+6=8$.

**Answer: 8**

nyciml-2009-10-fall-junior-08.title: Common index
nyciml-2009-10-fall-junior-08.body:
$\sqrt2\cdot\sqrt[3]3=2^{1/2}3^{1/3}=(2^3\cdot3^2)^{1/6}=\sqrt[6]{72}$. If $\sqrt[n]m$ equals this, then $m=72^{n/6}=2^{n/2}3^{n/3}$, which is an integer only when $2\mid n$ and $3\mid n$, i.e. $6\mid n$. The smallest is $n=6$, $m=72$.

**Answer: 72**

nyciml-2009-10-fall-junior-09.title: Pythagorean sums
nyciml-2009-10-fall-junior-09.body:
Let $E$ be the intersection of diagonals $AC$ and $BD$. The four triangles at $E$ are right, so $AB^2+CD^2=AE^2+BE^2+CE^2+DE^2=BC^2+DA^2$. Then $9+25=16+DA^2$, so $DA=\sqrt{18}=3\sqrt2$.

**Answer: $3\sqrt2$**

nyciml-2009-10-fall-junior-10.title: Self-similarity
nyciml-2009-10-fall-junior-10.body:
Let $x$ be the value. Then $x=\sqrt[3]{6+x}$, so $x^3-x-6=0$, which factors as $(x-2)(x^2+2x+3)=0$. The quadratic has negative discriminant, so the only real root is $x=2$.

**Answer: 2**

nyciml-2009-10-fall-junior-10.title: Inspection
nyciml-2009-10-fall-junior-10.body:
$\sqrt[3]{6+2}=2$, so $2$ is a fixed point, and the iterates $\sqrt[3]6\approx1.82$, $\sqrt[3]{7.82}\approx1.98,\dots$ approach it.

**Answer: 2**

nyciml-2009-10-fall-junior-11.title: Count the negatives
nyciml-2009-10-fall-junior-11.body:
The product is negative, so no factor is $0$ (automatic for odd numbers) and an odd number of factors are negative. Since $2008$ is even, not all are negative, so at least one is positive and $n\ge1$. With $n=1$ the numbers are $1,-1,-3,\dots,-4013$: $2007$ negatives, so the product is negative. Thus $n=1$.

**Answer: 1**

nyciml-2009-10-fall-junior-12.title: Choose a term from each factor
Trinomial triangle
nyciml-2009-10-fall-junior-12.body:
Build rows of coefficients of $(x^2+x+1)^k$: each entry is the sum of the three entries above it. The rows are $1,1,1$; $1,2,3,2,1$; $1,3,6,7,6,3,1$; $\dots$. The middle entry of row $9$ (the coefficient of $x^9$ in a degree-$18$ polynomial) is $3139$.

**Answer: 3139**

nyciml-2009-10-fall-junior-13.title: Use the signs
nyciml-2009-10-fall-junior-13.body:
The distinct factors must be among $\pm1,\pm2,\pm5,\pm10,\pm25,\pm50$. Since $50=2\cdot5^2$, at most one of $\pm2$ appears, and to use the most numbers we split $25$ as $5\cdot(-5)$ and include both $1$ and $-1$: $50=(-5)\cdot5\cdot2\cdot(-1)\cdot1$. More is impossible: apart from $\pm1$, each factor uses at least one prime factor, and $50$ has only three prime factors (with multiplicity), so at most $3+2=5$ integers.

**Answer: 5**

nyciml-2009-10-fall-junior-14.title: Two cases
nyciml-2009-10-fall-junior-14.body:
All odd: $5^4=625$. All even: the first digit can't be $0$, so $4\cdot5^3=500$. Total $1125$.

**Answer: 1125**

nyciml-2009-10-fall-junior-15.title: Set $x=1$
nyciml-2009-10-fall-junior-15.body:
The sum of the coefficients of a polynomial is its value at $x=1$: $(1+2+3+4)^3=1000$.

**Answer: 1000**

nyciml-2009-10-fall-junior-16.title: Power of a Point twice
nyciml-2009-10-fall-junior-16.body:
$K$ lies on the common chord $PQ$, so its power is the same for both circles: $AK\cdot KB=PK\cdot KQ=CK\cdot KD$. With $AK=7$: $7\cdot2=1\cdot KD$, so $KD=14$ and $BD=KD-KB=12$.

**Answer: 12**

nyciml-2009-10-fall-junior-17.title: Compare areas
nyciml-2009-10-fall-junior-17.body:
Let $O$ be the midpoint of $BC$ (the center), $r$ the radius and $h=OA$ the altitude. The semicircle has area $\frac12\pi r^2$ and the triangle $\frac12(2r)h=rh$. So $h=\frac{\pi r}{2}$ and $\tan\angle ABC=\frac hr=\frac\pi2$.

**Answer: $\frac{\pi}{2}$**

nyciml-2009-10-fall-junior-18.title: Distances from the center
nyciml-2009-10-fall-junior-18.body:
Let $a,b$ be the distances from the center to the sections of radii $8$ and $12$. Then $64+a^2=r^2=144+b^2$, so $(a-b)(a+b)=80$. If the sections are on the same side, $a-b=2$, so $a+b=40$ and $(a,b)=(21,19)$. If they are on opposite sides, $a+b=2$ forces $a-b=40$, impossible. So $r^2=64+441=505$ and $r=\sqrt{505}$.

**Answer: $\sqrt{505}$**
